**estirar** vs. **extender**: **estirar** suggests pulling/stretching something out; **extender** (to extend/spread) is used for more formal contexts.
Related: **el estiramiento** (the stretch/stretching) · **estirarse** (to stretch oneself — reflexive).
cards.englishPhrase: Stretch your arms.
cards.phrase: Estira los brazos.

cards.grammarNote:
**Sudo cuando corro** — both verbs are present tense, expressing habitual action (I sweat [whenever] I run).
Spanish uses present indicative in **cuando** clauses for habitual/repeated events.
Contrast: for future events, **cuando** takes the subjunctive: **Cuando corra mañana, sudaré** (When I run tomorrow, I'll sweat).
**sudar** (to sweat) · **el sudor** (sweat/perspiration) · **sudoroso** (sweaty).
cards.englishPhrase: I sweat when I run.
cards.phrase: Sudo cuando corro.

cards.grammarNote:
**¿Cómo te sientes?** uses **sentirse** (reflexive) for emotional/physical feeling: **me siento bien** (I feel well).
Contrast with non-reflexive **sentir** (to feel/sense something): **Siento un dolor** (I feel a pain).
**sentirse** conjugates like a reflexive: **me siento, te sientes, se siente, nos sentimos, os sentís, se sienten**.
**sentir** is an e→ie stem-changer in the present: **siento, sientes, siente**.
cards.englishPhrase: How do you feel?
cards.phrase: ¿Cómo te sientes?

cards.grammarNote:
**pensar** is an e→ie stem-changing verb — changes in all forms except nosotros/vosotros:
**pienso · piensas · piensa · pensamos · pensáis · piensan**
Other e→ie verbs: **querer** (quiero) · **entender** (entiendo) · **empezar** (empiezo) · **perder** (pierdo)
cards.englishPhrase: What are you thinking about?
cards.phrase: ¿En qué piensas?

cards.grammarNote:
**mover** is an o→ue stem-changing verb: **muevo, mueves, mueve, movemos, movéis, mueven**.
**No puedo mover el brazo** — note **el brazo** (the arm) with definite article, not *mi brazo*.
**poder** (can/to be able to) is also o→ue: **puedo, puedes, puede**.
Reflexive **moverse** = to move (oneself): **No puedo moverme** (I can't move).
cards.englishPhrase: I can't move my arm.
cards.phrase: No puedo mover el brazo.

cards.grammarNote:
**suave** is invariable for gender — same form for masculine and feminine: **el tejido suave** / **la piel suave**.
**ser** vs. **estar** with **suave**: **El tejido es suave** (the tissue is soft — inherent property, use **ser**) vs. **El tejido está suave** (the tissue feels soft — current/perceived state, use **estar**).
Related: **suavidad** (softness) · **suavizar** (to soften) · **suavemente** (softly, gently).
cards.englishPhrase: The tissue is soft.
cards.phrase: El tejido es suave.

cards.grammarNote:
**Tengo los músculos doloridos** — **tener + los + body part (plural) + adjective** for physical states.
**dolorido** (sore/aching) comes from **dolor** (pain) — related to **doler** (to hurt) and **doloroso** (painful).
The adjective **doloridos** agrees in gender (masculine) and number (plural) with **los músculos**.
Common after exercise: **tengo las piernas doloridas** (my legs are sore).
cards.englishPhrase: My muscles are sore.
cards.phrase: Tengo los músculos doloridos.

cards.grammarNote:
**izquierdo/izquierda** (left) comes from Basque **ezker** — one of the few Basque loanwords in Spanish.
Adjectives of direction follow the noun: **la rodilla izquierda** (the left knee), **el brazo derecho** (the right arm).
**izquierda** agrees in gender (feminine) with **la rodilla**.
Common expressions: **a la izquierda** (to the left) · **de izquierdas** (left-wing, politically).
cards.englishPhrase: I hurt my left knee.
cards.phrase: Me duele la rodilla izquierda.

cards.grammarNote:
**derecho/derecha** (right direction) also means 'straight' and 'right' (legal/moral): **los derechos humanos** (human rights), **ir derecho** (to go straight).
**Me rompí el brazo derecho** — reflexive injury pattern with definite article: the **me** shows whose arm, so **el** not *mi*.
**derecho** agrees in gender (masculine) with **el brazo**.
Distinction: **derecho** (adjective, right/straight) vs. **a la derecha** (to the right — directional phrase).
cards.englishPhrase: I broke my right arm.
cards.phrase: Me rompí el brazo derecho.

cards.grammarNote:
**superior** is invariable for gender — same form for masculine and feminine nouns.
**la parte superior del cuerpo** — **del** is a contraction of **de + el**: *de el* → **del**.
**ser** is used here (**es fuerte**) because strength is an inherent characteristic of the upper body — not a temporary state.
Opposite: **inferior** (lower) — both are Latin-derived adjectives, same in English.
cards.englishPhrase: The upper body is strong.
cards.phrase: La parte superior del cuerpo es fuerte.

cards.grammarNote:
**inferior** is invariable for gender — same form for masculine and feminine nouns.
**tener dolor en la parte inferior de la espalda** — note **en** (in/at) before the specific location; compare **tener dolor de espalda** (general back pain) without **en**.
**del** (de + el) is used for contractions, but here the article is **la** (feminine), so no contraction: **de la espalda**.
Opposite: **superior** (upper) — both invariable adjectives from Latin.
cards.englishPhrase: He has lower back pain.
cards.phrase: Él tiene dolor en la parte inferior de la espalda.

cards.grammarNote:
Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, and the article agrees:
**el** (masc.) · **la** (fem.) → **el pan** (bread), **la leche** (milk). Most **-o** words are masculine, most **-a** feminine — but learn each noun with its article.
cards.englishPhrase: The bread is here, the milk is there.
cards.phrase: El pan está aquí, la leche está allí.

table.title: Definite articles agree with gender & number
table.note: Most -o words are masculine, most -a feminine — learn each noun with its article.

cards.grammarNote:
Spanish usually **drops the subject pronoun** — the verb ending already shows who the subject is.
**Soy estudiante** = **Yo soy estudiante**. Add **yo/tú/él** only for emphasis or contrast.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm a student, and you?
cards.phrase: Soy estudiante, ¿y tú?

table.title: ser — the subject pronoun is optional
table.note: The ending already shows who — add yo/tú/él only for emphasis.

cards.grammarNote:
Adjectives agree in gender and number with who they describe:
**él está nervioso** / **ella está nerviosa** / **ellos están nerviosos**. Change the ending **-o** (masc.) ↔ **-a** (fem.), add **-s** for plural.
cards.englishPhrase: The girls are tired.
cards.phrase: Las chicas están cansadas.

produce.concept: Adjectives match the noun they modify
produce.task: he is nervous, she is nervous
produce.answer: él está nervioso, ella está nerviosa

cards.english: I am a doctor. (no article before jobs)
cards.grammarNote:
State a profession with **ser** and **no article**:
**soy médico** (I'm a doctor), **es profesora** (she's a teacher). Add an article only with a description: **es un buen médico** (he's a good doctor).
cards.englishPhrase: She is an engineer.
cards.phrase: Ella es ingeniera.

cards.english: The bank is nearby. (estar for location)
cards.grammarNote:
Location always uses **estar**, even for permanent buildings:
**el banco está cerca** (the bank is nearby), **¿dónde está el baño?** (where's the bathroom?). Never **es** for location.
cards.englishPhrase: Where is the museum?
cards.phrase: ¿Dónde está el museo?

cards.english: The food is delicious. (estar for taste)
cards.grammarNote:
Use **estar** (not **ser**) for how food tastes right now — a temporary state:
**la comida está deliciosa** (the food is delicious), **el café está frío** (the coffee is cold). **ser** would sound like a permanent trait.
cards.englishPhrase: This soup is very good!
cards.phrase: ¡Esta sopa está muy buena!

b.gloss: a good soup in general → ser

a.gloss: I feel happy right now — a mood (estar)

b.gloss: I'm a happy person — a trait (ser)

cards.grammarNote:
Feelings and moods use **estar** — they're temporary states:
**estoy feliz** (I'm happy), **estoy triste** (I'm sad). **ser feliz** exists too, but describes being a happy person in general.
cards.englishPhrase: Are you okay? — I'm fine.
cards.phrase: ¿Estás bien? — Estoy bien.

cards.english: There's a bank / The bank is here (hay vs estar)
cards.word: hay un banco / el banco está aquí
cards.grammarNote:
**hay** introduces something that exists (indefinite): **hay un banco cerca**. **estar** locates something already known (definite): **el banco está en la esquina**.
Rule of thumb: **hay** + un/una/números; **estar** + el/la/mi/este.
cards.englishPhrase: There's a pharmacy nearby, and the pharmacy is on the corner.
cards.phrase: Hay una farmacia cerca, y la farmacia está en la esquina.

a.gloss: a bank exists / introduces it → hay

b.gloss: the known bank is located here → estar

cards.grammarNote:
**hay** = there is / there are — one word for both singular and plural:
**hay pan** (there's bread), **hay dos manzanas** (there are two apples). It never changes form.
cards.englishPhrase: Is there water?
cards.phrase: ¿Hay agua?

table.title: hay — there is / there are (invariable)
table.note: One form for all — hay never changes.

cards.english: you (formal — to a stranger or elder)
cards.grammarNote:
Two words for 'you': **tú** (informal — friends, kids) · **usted** (formal — strangers, elders, bosses).
**usted** takes the **él/ella** verb form: **usted tiene**, not *usted tienes*.
cards.englishPhrase: How are you? (formal)
cards.phrase: ¿Cómo está usted?

cards.grammarNote:
Spanish **has** a feeling where English **is** one — use **tener**, not ser/estar:
**tengo hambre** (hungry) · **tengo sed** (thirsty) · **tengo frío/calor** (cold/hot) · **tengo miedo** (afraid) · **tengo 20 años** (I'm 20).
cards.englishPhrase: I'm cold and hungry.
cards.phrase: Tengo frío y hambre.

table.title: Physical states use tener (‘to have’)
table.note: Spanish ‘has’ the state where English ‘is’ it — not ser/estar.

cards.grammarNote:
Some feelings use **tener** (to have), not **estar**:
**tengo miedo** (I'm afraid), **tengo celos** (I'm jealous), **tengo sueño** (I'm sleepy). Literally 'I have fear/jealousy/sleepiness'.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm a little afraid.
cards.phrase: Tengo un poco de miedo.

table.title: More tener idioms (not estar)
table.note: Literally ‘I have fear / sleep / hurry…’.

cards.english: I have cold hands. (tener + article + agreement)
cards.grammarNote:
Describe your body with **tener** + article + adjective (which agrees):
**tengo las manos frías** (my hands are cold, lit. 'I have the hands cold'), **tiene los ojos azules** (she has blue eyes).
cards.englishPhrase: She has blue eyes.
cards.phrase: Ella tiene los ojos azules.

cloze.prompt: my hands are cold (las manos = fem. pl.)

cards.english: I like coffee. (gustar works in reverse)
cards.grammarNote:
**gustar** literally means 'to please' — the thing liked is the subject:
**me gusta el café** = 'coffee pleases me'. Use **gusta** for one thing, **gustan** for plural: **me gustan las manzanas**.
cards.englishPhrase: I like tea, and you?
cards.phrase: Me gusta el té, ¿y a ti?

table.title: gustar — ‘to please’ (works backwards)
table.note: One thing → gusta; plural things → gustan (me gustan las uvas).

cards.grammarNote:
To say you like doing something, use **me gusta** + the infinitive:
**me gusta leer** (I like reading), **me gusta correr** (I like running). Stays singular **gusta** before a verb.
cards.englishPhrase: I like listening to music.
cards.phrase: Me gusta escuchar música.

cloze.prompt: I like reading (a verb → stays singular)

cards.english: My head hurts. (me duele — like gustar)
cards.grammarNote:
**doler** (to hurt) works like **gustar** — the body part is the subject:
**me duele la cabeza** (my head hurts), **me duelen los pies** (my feet hurt — plural **duelen**). Uses the article, not 'my'.
cards.englishPhrase: My stomach hurts.
cards.phrase: Me duele el estómago.

table.title: doler — works like gustar
table.note: Body part is the subject → duele / duelen; use the article, not ‘my’.

cards.english: What's your name? (lit. how do you call yourself)
cards.grammarNote:
Names use the reflexive verb **llamarse** ('to call oneself'):
**me llamo** (I call myself) · **te llamas** (you call yourself) · **se llama** (he/she calls him/herself).
cards.englishPhrase: What's your name? — My name is Ana.
cards.phrase: ¿Cómo te llamas? — Me llamo Ana.

table.title: llamarse — ‘to call oneself’ (names)
table.note: ¿Cómo te llamas? = What's your name?

cards.grammarNote:
With body parts, Spanish uses the **definite article** (el/la/los/las), not a possessive — the reflexive pronoun already shows whose:
**me lavo las manos** (I wash my hands), **le duele la cabeza** (his head hurts). Not *mis manos*.
cards.englishPhrase: I brush my teeth.
cards.phrase: Me cepillo los dientes.

contrast.prompt: ‘I wash my hands’ — las or mis?

a.gloss: ✓ reflexive already shows it's yours → article

cards.grammarNote:
**sentirse** (to feel) is reflexive — the pronoun matches the subject:
**me siento** (I feel), **te sientes** (you feel), **se siente** (he/she feels). In **me siento cansado/cansada** the adjective still agrees.
cards.englishPhrase: How do you feel? — I feel great.
cards.phrase: ¿Cómo te sientes? — Me siento genial.

table.title: sentirse — ‘to feel’ (reflexive, e→ie)
table.note: Adjective still agrees: me siento cansado / cansada.

cards.grammarNote:
Two mandatory contractions before masculine **el**:
**a + el → al** (Voy **al** parque), **de + el → del** (la puerta **del** hotel). They don't contract with **la/los/las**.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm going to the market from the office.
cards.phrase: Voy al mercado desde la oficina.

produce.concept: el contracts: a + el → al, de + el → del
produce.task: I'm going to the park; the hotel door
produce.answer: voy al parque; la puerta del hotel
produce.gloss: Only masculine singular el contracts — never la/los/las.

cards.english: I'm going to the park. (ir a + place)
cards.grammarNote:
**ir a** + place = to go to a place; remember **a + el → al**:
**voy al parque** (I go to the park), **vamos a la playa** (we go to the beach). Also **ir a** + infinitive = near future: **voy a comer**.
cards.englishPhrase: We're going to the beach today.
cards.phrase: Hoy vamos a la playa.

cards.grammarNote:
The present progressive = **estar** + gerund (**-ando** / **-iendo**):
**estoy nadando** (I'm swimming), **estoy comiendo** (I'm eating). Only for actions happening right now.
cards.englishPhrase: She is reading now.
cards.phrase: Ella está leyendo ahora.

table.title: Present progressive: estar + gerund
table.note: estoy nadando = I'm swimming (right now).

table.title: querer — to want (e→ie)
table.note: Stem e→ie in the stressed forms; nosotros keeps the e.

cards.grammarNote:
**querer** is a stem-changing verb: e→ie in the stressed forms.
**quiero · quieres · quiere · queremos · quieren** — note **nosotros queremos** keeps the **e** (unstressed).
cards.englishPhrase: Do you want a coffee?
cards.phrase: ¿Quieres un café?

cards.grammarNote:
**la mano** is feminine even though it ends in **-o** — a classic exception:
**la mano derecha** (the right hand). Other tricky ones: **el día** (masc., ends -a), **el problema** (masc.).
cards.englishPhrase: Give me your right hand.
cards.phrase: Dame la mano derecha.

table.title: Gender exceptions
table.note: These break the -o/-a rule; memorize them.

cards.english: I work as a nurse. (trabajar de/como)
cards.grammarNote:
**trabajar de** or **trabajar como** = to work as (a job):
**trabajo de enfermero** (I work as a nurse), **trabajo en un hospital** (I work in a hospital — **en** for the place).
cards.englishPhrase: I work as a cook in a restaurant.
cards.phrase: Trabajo de cocinero en un restaurante.

table.title: Talking about your job
table.note: de / como = work AS; en = work IN / at a place.

cards.grammarNote: The **preterite** is the narrative past — a single, completed action seen as finished. Regular **-ar** verbs take the endings **-é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -aron**. Only **yo** and **él/ella** carry a written accent.
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I worked at the office.
cards.phrase: Ayer trabajé en la oficina.

table.title: Preterite: -ar verbs (trabajar)
table.note: Accents only on trabajé and trabajó.

cards.grammarNote: **-er** and **-ir** verbs share the *same* preterite endings: **-í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -ieron**. So comer and vivir conjugate identically.
cards.englishPhrase: Last night I ate at the restaurant.
cards.phrase: Anoche comí en el restaurante.

table.title: Preterite: -er / -ir (comer, vivir)
table.note: -er and -ir are identical in the preterite.

cards.grammarNote: For a finished, one-time action use the preterite. The **él/ella** form of an -ar verb ends in **-ó** (cocinó), never the present **-a** (cocina).
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday she cooked dinner.
cards.phrase: Ayer ella cocinó la cena.

cards.english: I went to the park. (ir → fui)
cards.grammarNote: **ser** and **ir** have the *same* irregular preterite: **fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fueron** — context tells them apart. **Fui al parque** = I went; **fui médico** = I was a doctor.
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I went to the park.
cards.phrase: Ayer fui al parque.

table.title: Preterite: ser AND ir (identical)
table.note: No accents. Context decides 'went' vs 'was'.

cards.english: I was at home last night. (estar → estuve)
cards.grammarNote: A group of irregulars takes a new stem + the endings **-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron** (no accents): **estar→estuv-, tener→tuv-, poder→pud-**. So: estuve, tuve, pude.
cards.englishPhrase: Last night I was at home.
cards.phrase: Anoche estuve en casa.

table.title: Irregular preterite (new stem, -e/-o)
table.note: Endings: -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron. No accent on yo/él.

cards.grammarNote: More irregular stems, same **-e/-o** endings: **hacer→hic-** (but **hizo** with z), **decir→dij-** (dijeron, no i), **venir→vin-**.
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I made dinner.
cards.phrase: Ayer hice la cena.

table.title: Irregular preterite (hacer, decir, venir)
table.note: hizo spelled with z; dijeron drops the i.

cards.english: Say the preterite 'yo' form. (I ate / drank / lived)
cards.grammarNote: The **yo** preterite of regular -er/-ir verbs ends in a stressed **-í**: comer→comí, beber→bebí, vivir→viví.
cards.englishPhrase: I ate, I drank, I lived.
cards.phrase: Comí, bebí, viví.

produce.concept: Preterite = one finished action in the past
produce.task: I ate, I drank, I lived

cards.english: As a child I used to swim. (imperfect, -ar)
cards.grammarNote: The **imperfect** is the 'used to / was ‑ing' past — habits and background, no clear end. Regular **-ar** verbs take **-aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -aban**.
cards.englishPhrase: As a child I used to swim at the beach.
cards.phrase: De niño nadaba en la playa.

table.title: Imperfect: -ar verbs (nadar)
table.note: yo and él/ella are identical: nadaba.

cards.english: As a child I used to eat a lot of bread. (imperfect, -er/-ir)
cards.grammarNote: **-er** and **-ir** verbs share the imperfect endings **-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían** — every form carries an accent on the **í**.
cards.englishPhrase: As a child I used to eat a lot of bread.
cards.phrase: De niño comía mucho pan.

table.title: Imperfect: -er / -ir (comer, vivir)
table.note: Accent on every í. -er and -ir identical.

cards.english: As a child I was happy. (ser → era)
cards.grammarNote: The imperfect has only **three** irregular verbs: **ser→era, ir→iba, ver→veía**. Learn these; everything else is regular.
cards.englishPhrase: As a child I was happy.
cards.phrase: De niño era feliz.

table.title: The 3 irregular imperfects
table.note: The ONLY irregular imperfect verbs.

cards.english: She always cooked at home. (habit → imperfect)
cards.grammarNote: Words like **siempre** (always) and **nunca** (never) signal a repeated habit → use the **imperfect** (cocinaba), not the preterite (cocinó).
cards.englishPhrase: She always cooked at home.
cards.phrase: Siempre cocinaba en casa.

cards.english: Say the imperfect. (I used to work / she used to study)
cards.grammarNote: Imperfect = 'used to' or 'would' (habitual). -ar yo/él ends in **-aba**: trabajaba, estudiaba.
cards.englishPhrase: I used to work, she used to study.
cards.phrase: Trabajaba, estudiaba.

produce.concept: Imperfect = used to / would (a past habit)
produce.task: I used to work, she used to study

cards.english: I ate out — once vs. every day.
cards.grammarNote: Same verb, two pasts: **preterite** = one finished event; **imperfect** = a repeated habit or ongoing background. **Comí** (I ate, that once) vs **comía** (I used to eat).
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I ate out; as a child I ate at home.
cards.phrase: Ayer comí en el restaurante; de niño comía en casa.

cards.grammarNote: The time expression usually decides the tense. **ayer, anoche, la semana pasada** → a finished point → **preterite**. **siempre, de niño** → a habit → **imperfect**.
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I worked; as a child I worked here.
cards.phrase: Ayer trabajé; de niño trabajaba.

table.title: Which past does the time word want?
table.note: A fixed point → preterite; a habit → imperfect.

cards.english: I was cooking when she arrived. (background + event)
cards.grammarNote: For an interrupted scene, the ongoing background is **imperfect** (cocinaba) and the event that cuts in is **preterite** (llegó). English 'was ‑ing' → imperfect.
cards.englishPhrase: I was cooking when she arrived.
cards.phrase: Cocinaba cuando llegó.

cloze.prompt: I was cooking (ongoing) when she arrived

cards.english: I arrived, cooked, and ate. (a chain of events)
cards.grammarNote: A sequence of completed actions, each moving the story forward, is all **preterite**: llegué, cociné, comí. (Note llegar → **llegué** keeps the hard g with -ué.)
cards.englishPhrase: I arrived, I cooked, and I ate.
cards.phrase: Llegué, cociné y comí.

produce.concept: A chain of finished actions → all preterite
produce.task: I arrived, I cooked, and I ate
produce.gloss: each completed step moves the story → preterite

cards.english: Tomorrow I'm going to study at home. (near/planned future: ir a + infinitive)
cards.word: mañana voy a estudiar en casa
cards.grammarNote: The **near future** is **ir a + infinitive**: conjugate *ir* (voy, vas, va, vamos, van) and add **a** plus an unchanged infinitive. It's the most common way to talk about plans in speech.
cards.englishPhrase: Tomorrow I'm going to study at home.
cards.phrase: Mañana voy a estudiar en casa.

table.title: ir a + infinitive (near future)
table.note: Only ir changes; the infinitive stays the same.

cards.english: Tomorrow I will speak with María. (simple future)
cards.grammarNote: The **simple future** adds one set of endings to the *whole infinitive* — same for -ar, -er, -ir: **-é, -ás, -á, -emos, -án**. hablar → hablaré, comer → comeré, vivir → viviré.
cards.englishPhrase: Tomorrow I will speak with María.
cards.phrase: Mañana hablaré con María.

table.title: Simple future (endings on the infinitive)
table.note: Same endings for -ar/-er/-ir. Accent on every form except nosotros.

cards.english: Tomorrow I will eat at the restaurant. (future -er)
cards.grammarNote: Future endings attach to the **full infinitive**, so -er/-ir verbs work the same way: comer → **comeré**, vivir → **viviré**.
cards.englishPhrase: Tomorrow I will eat at the restaurant.
cards.phrase: Mañana comeré en el restaurante.

cards.english: Tomorrow I will have to work. (irregular future stems)
cards.grammarNote: Some verbs use an **irregular future stem** but take the **normal endings**: tener→**tendr-**, poder→**podr-**, salir→**saldr-**, hacer→**har-**, decir→**dir-**. So tener → tendré, tendrás, tendrá...
cards.englishPhrase: Tomorrow I will have to work.
cards.phrase: Mañana tendré que trabajar.

table.title: Irregular future stems (+ normal endings)
table.note: Stem changes, but the endings (-é, -ás, -á...) are the same.

cards.english: going to eat vs. will eat
cards.grammarNote: **ir a + infinitive** = a near, planned future (very common in speech). The **simple future** (-é) feels a bit more distant or formal. Both are correct.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm going to eat now; tomorrow I will eat at home.
cards.phrase: Voy a comer ahora; mañana comeré en casa.

cards.english: Say the future 'yo' form. (I will eat / drink / live)
cards.grammarNote: The **yo** future ends in a stressed **-é** on the full infinitive: comer→comeré, beber→beberé, vivir→viviré.
cards.englishPhrase: I will eat, I will drink, I will live.
cards.phrase: Comeré, beberé, viviré.

produce.task: I will eat, I will drink, I will live

cards.english: He's probably at home. (future of probability / a guess about the present)
cards.grammarNote: The **future** can express **probability about the present** — a guess, not a plan. *Está en casa* = I know he's home; *estará en casa* = he's **probably** home. Often answers ¿Dónde estará? (Where can he be?).
cards.englishPhrase: He is at home (I know); he's probably at home (a guess).
cards.phrase: Está en casa; estará en casa.

contrast.prompt: Fact you know or a guess?

cards.english: Tomorrow I will go to the park. (future of ir)
cards.grammarNote: *ir* is **regular** in the future: it takes the normal endings on the infinitive → **iré, irás, irá, iremos, irán**.
cards.englishPhrase: Tomorrow I will go to the park.
cards.phrase: Mañana yo iré al parque.

cards.grammarNote: The **conditional** ('would') adds one set of endings to the *whole infinitive* — same for -ar/-er/-ir: **-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían**. hablar → hablaría.
cards.englishPhrase: I would speak with María.
cards.phrase: Yo hablaría con María.

table.title: Conditional (endings on the infinitive)
table.note: Accent on every í. yo and él/ella match.

cards.english: I would eat at the restaurant. (conditional -er)
cards.grammarNote: Conditional endings attach to the **full infinitive**, so -er/-ir behave the same: comer → **comería**, vivir → **viviría**.
cards.englishPhrase: I would eat at the restaurant.
cards.phrase: Yo comería en el restaurante.

cards.english: I would have to work more. (irregular conditional)
cards.grammarNote: Some verbs use an **irregular stem** — the *same* stem as the future — then add **-ía**. tener → **tendría**, hacer → **haría**, poder → **podría**, salir → **saldría**, decir → **diría**.
cards.englishPhrase: I would have to work more.
cards.phrase: Yo tendría que trabajar más.

table.title: Irregular conditional stems (same as future) + -ía
table.note: Learn the stem once; future and conditional share it.

cards.english: I want a coffee vs. I would like a coffee
cards.grammarNote: The **conditional softens** requests to sound polite. Blunt: **quiero** (I want). Polite: **me gustaría** (I would like), **¿podrías...?** (could you...?).
cards.englishPhrase: I want a coffee → I would like a coffee, please.
cards.phrase: Quiero un café → Me gustaría un café.

cards.english: Say the wish: I would live at the beach; I would travel a lot.
cards.word: viviría en la playa; viajaría mucho
cards.grammarNote: The **conditional** expresses hypotheticals and wishes ('would'). vivir → **viviría**, viajar → **viajaría** — regular -ía on the full infinitive.
cards.englishPhrase: I would live at the beach; I would travel a lot.
cards.phrase: Viviría en la playa; viajaría mucho.

produce.task: I would live at the beach; I would travel a lot
produce.answer: viviría en la playa; viajaría mucho

cards.english: Say the conditional 'yo' form. (I would eat / drink / live)
cards.grammarNote: The **yo** conditional ends in **-ía** on the full infinitive: comer→comería, beber→bebería, vivir→viviría.
cards.englishPhrase: I would eat, I would drink, I would live.
cards.phrase: Comería, bebería, viviría.

produce.task: I would eat, I would drink, I would live

cards.english: I will eat vs. I would eat
cards.grammarNote: Future and conditional share the same stem; only the endings differ. Future **-é** = 'will' (comeré). Conditional **-ía** = 'would' (comería).
cards.englishPhrase: Tomorrow I will eat; I would eat more, but I can't.
cards.phrase: Mañana comeré; comería más, pero no puedo.

cards.english: I would go to the park, but I can't. (conditional of ir)
cards.grammarNote: **ir** is regular in the conditional: add **-ía** to the infinitive → **iría** (I would go). Don't confuse it with the future **iré** (I will go).
cards.englishPhrase: I would go to the park, but I can't.
cards.phrase: Yo iría al parque, pero no puedo.

cloze.text: yo ___ al parque, pero no puedo

cards.english: Direct object pronouns — the full set (me / te / lo·la / nos / los·las)
cards.grammarNote:
A **direct object** receives the action of the verb. Replace it with a **direct object pronoun** that matches the person (and gender/number for third person). The pronoun goes **before** the conjugated verb.

**¿El café? Lo quiero.** → *lo* replaces *el café*.
cards.englishPhrase: The coffee? I want it.
cards.phrase: ¿El café? Lo quiero.

table.title: Direct object pronouns
table.note: lo/la and los/las must match the gender and number of the noun they replace.

cards.english: lo/la replaces a noun to avoid repetition (it — the bread / the salad)
cards.grammarNote:
To avoid repeating a noun, replace it with **lo** (masculine) or **la** (feminine). The pronoun goes **before** the conjugated verb.

*Compro el pan.* → **Lo** compro. | *Compro la ensalada.* → **La** compro.
cards.englishPhrase: I buy the bread. → I buy it.
cards.phrase: Compro el pan. → Lo compro.

cards.english: lo/la/los/las must match the gender AND number of the noun replaced
cards.grammarNote:
**lo** = masc. singular (el pan, el queso…)
**la** = fem. singular (la ensalada, la leche…)
**los** = masc. plural (los huevos, los platos…)
**las** = fem. plural (las galletas, las manzanas…)

Always match the replaced noun, not the English 'it/them'.
cards.englishPhrase: The bread — I want it. The salad — I want it. The cookies — I want them.
cards.phrase: El pan — lo quiero. La ensalada — la quiero. Las galletas — las quiero.

produce.task: Give the correct pronoun for: the bread (masc. sg.), the salad (fem. sg.), the cookies (fem. pl.)
produce.gloss: lo → masc. sg. | la → fem. sg. | las → fem. pl.

cards.english: Pronoun placement: before a conjugated verb OR attached to an infinitive (both correct)
cards.grammarNote:
With **conjugated verb + infinitive**, the direct object pronoun has two equally correct positions:
1. **Before the conjugated verb**: *Lo quiero comprar.*
2. **Attached to the infinitive**: *Quiero comprarlo.*

Both mean the same thing.
cards.englishPhrase: I want to buy it.
cards.phrase: Lo quiero comprar. / Quiero comprarlo.

contrast.prompt: Both are correct — where does 'lo' go?

cards.english: With estar + gerund, pronoun attaches to the gerund (with accent) OR goes before estar
cards.grammarNote:
With **estar + gerund**, the direct object pronoun has two positions:
1. **Before estar**: *Lo estoy mirando.*
2. **Attached to the gerund** (written accent required): *Estoy **mirándolo**.*

When you attach the pronoun, add an accent to keep the original stress on the gerund.
cards.englishPhrase: I am watching it.
cards.phrase: Lo estoy mirando. / Estoy mirándolo.

cloze.prompt: I am watching it — attach the pronoun to the gerund

cards.grammarNote: The **indirect object pronoun** marks the recipient — 'to/for whom'. It goes **before** the conjugated verb. **me** = to me, **te** = to you, **le** = to him/her/usted, **nos** = to us, **les** = to them.
cards.englishPhrase: I give the menu to him (the waiter).
cards.phrase: Le doy el menú al camarero.

table.title: Indirect Object Pronouns
table.note: Pronoun goes before the conjugated verb.

cards.english: le = to him/her with dar and decir
cards.grammarNote: Use **le** when the recipient is 'him', 'her', or 'usted'. It always goes **before** the verb: **le** doy, **le** digo, **le** escribo.
cards.englishPhrase: I give the cake to María.
cards.phrase: Le doy el pastel a María.

cloze.prompt: to her (María) — I give the cake

cards.word: Le doy el café a María.
cards.grammarNote: In Spanish, **le** and **a + person** are used **together**. The pronoun (le/les) is required even when you also name the person with 'a'. This is normal, not redundant.
cards.englishPhrase: I give the coffee to María.
cards.phrase: Le doy el café a María.

produce.task: Say 'I give the coffee to María' — use both le and a María.
produce.answer: Le doy el café a María.
produce.gloss: le + a María together is normal in Spanish — the pronoun is never dropped

cards.english: gustar in reverse: IO pronoun marks who likes it
cards.word: me gusta / te gusta / le gusta
cards.grammarNote: With **gustar**, the thing liked is the **subject** (gusta = singular, gustan = plural). The IO pronoun marks **who** likes it. So: 'I like coffee' = **me gusta** el café (literally: coffee pleases me).
cards.englishPhrase: She likes the coffee.
cards.phrase: A ella le gusta el café.

table.title: gustar — reverse verb
table.note: gusta = one thing liked; gustan = multiple things liked.

cards.english: doler (to hurt) follows the same pattern as gustar
cards.grammarNote: **doler** works like gustar — the IO pronoun marks who feels the pain, and the verb agrees with the body part. **me duele** (one part) vs. **me duelen** (plural: los pies, las manos).
cards.englishPhrase: My head hurts. (My feet hurt.)
cards.phrase: Me duele la cabeza. (Me duelen los pies.)

cards.english: lo (direct) vs. le (indirect): sees him vs. gives to him
cards.word: lo veo / le doy el café
cards.grammarNote: **lo** = direct object — the person/thing directly receiving the action (who/what is seen, bought, etc.). **le** = indirect object — the recipient of something ('to/for whom'). When you give, say, or write *something* **to** someone, that 'someone' gets **le**.
cards.englishPhrase: I see him; I give him the coffee.
cards.phrase: Lo veo; le doy el café.

contrast.prompt: Which pronoun: sees him (direct) or gives to him (indirect)?

b.gloss: I give him the coffee → indirect object / recipient (le)

cards.english: Double object pronouns: indirect always comes first
cards.word: me lo / te la / nos los
cards.grammarNote: When a sentence has TWO object pronouns, the **indirect pronoun comes first**, then the direct: **indirect + direct**.
cards.englishPhrase: The coffee? The waiter gives it to me.
cards.phrase: ¿El café? Me lo da el camarero.

table.title: Two pronouns: indirect + direct
table.note: Order is always: indirect first, then direct.

cards.english: le/les + lo/la → se lo / se la (never le lo)
cards.grammarNote: When **le** or **les** appears before **lo / la / los / las**, the **le/les becomes se**. **Le lo** is never allowed → always **se lo**.
cards.englishPhrase: The menu? I give it to María.
cards.phrase: ¿El menú? Se lo doy a María.

cloze.text: El menú, a María → ___ lo doy.

cards.word: se lo doy / se lo dice
cards.grammarNote: **le** or **les** + **lo/la** → **se lo / se la**. The indirect object can be clarified with 'a + name': **se lo doy a María**.
cards.englishPhrase: I give it (the coffee) to María. He tells it to her.
cards.phrase: Se lo doy a María. Él se lo dice.

produce.task: Give it (the coffee) to María; tell it to her.
produce.answer: Se lo doy a María. Él se lo dice.
produce.gloss: le + lo is never allowed → se lo; indirect always first

cards.english: Double pronouns: before conjugated verb OR attached to infinitive
cards.word: te lo quiero dar / quiero dártelo
cards.grammarNote: With an infinitive, both pronouns can go **before the conjugated verb** (separate) or **attached together to the infinitive** (add written accent).
cards.englishPhrase: I want to give it to you.
cards.phrase: Te lo quiero dar. / Quiero dártelo.

contrast.prompt: Where do the double pronouns go with an infinitive?

cards.english: Full production: order + se lo rule together
cards.word: te lo compro / se la doy
cards.grammarNote: Combine both rules: **indirect first + direct second**, and **le → se** before lo/la. El pastel (masc.) → **lo**; la cuenta (fem.) → **la**.
cards.englishPhrase: I buy it (the cake) for you. I give it (the bill) to the waiter.
cards.phrase: Te lo compro. Se la doy al camarero.

produce.task: I buy it (the cake) for you; I give it (the bill) to the waiter.
produce.answer: Te lo compro. Se la doy al camarero.
produce.gloss: el pastel → lo (masc.); la cuenta → la (fem.); le + la → se la

cards.grammarNote:
**el** Spanish sports names often take the masculine definite article *el*.
**cognate** Píckleball is an English loanword adopted directly into Spanish.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey plays pickleball every weekend.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey juega al píckleball todos los fines de semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**la** Feminine noun; most nouns ending in *-a* are feminine.
**jugar con** To play *with* an instrument uses the preposition *con*.
cards.englishPhrase: My paddle is red and black.
cards.phrase: Mi pala es roja y negra.

cards.grammarNote:
**la cancha** Common in Latin America; Spain often says *la pista*.
**estar en** Location uses *estar*, not *ser*, because it is temporary.
cards.englishPhrase: We reserved the court for two hours.
cards.phrase: Reservamos la cancha por dos horas.

cards.grammarNote:
**sacar** Used for the action of serving; literally 'to take out'.
**el saque** The noun form meaning 'the serve' or 'the serve shot'.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey has a very strong serve.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey tiene un saque muy fuerte.

cards.grammarNote:
**el peloteo** Derived from *pelota* (ball); describes the back-and-forth exchange.
**durar** Use *durar* to say how long a rally lasts.
cards.englishPhrase: That rally lasted twenty shots.
cards.phrase: Ese peloteo duró veinte golpes.

cards.grammarNote:
**el marcador** Refers to the scoreboard or the current score.
**llevar** *Llevar* means 'to carry' but *llevar el marcador* means 'to keep score'.
cards.englishPhrase: What is the score?
cards.phrase: ¿Cuál es el marcador?

cards.grammarNote:
**anotar** To score a point you use *anotar un punto* or *marcar un punto*.
**plural** *Los puntos* follows the regular masculine plural rule.
cards.englishPhrase: I scored the winning point!
cards.phrase: ¡Anoté el punto ganador!

cards.grammarNote:
**el partido** The standard word for a sports match or game in Spanish.
**jugar un partido** Literally 'to play a match'; *jugar* always pairs with *a + definite article* before a sport.
cards.englishPhrase: We played a great match yesterday.
cards.phrase: Ayer jugamos un partido increíble.

cards.grammarNote:
**el torneo** Masculine noun; comes from Old French *tornei*.
**participar en** To take part in a tournament use *participar en el torneo*.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey signed up for the local tournament.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey se inscribió en el torneo local.

cards.grammarNote:
**el oponente** A direct loanword from English/Latin; formal usage.
**el rival** More commonly used in everyday Spanish sports talk.
cards.englishPhrase: My opponent was very fast.
cards.phrase: Mi rival era muy rápido.

cards.grammarNote:
**ganar** A regular -ar verb meaning 'to win' or 'to earn'.
**ganamos** The *nosotros* preterite is the same form as the present, so context clarifies tense.
cards.englishPhrase: We won the match against my brothers!
cards.phrase: ¡Ganamos el partido contra mis hermanos!

cards.grammarNote:
**perder** An *e→ie* stem-changing verb in the present tense (*pierdo*, *pierdes*…).
**no pasa nada** A common consolation phrase meaning 'no worries / it's okay'.
cards.englishPhrase: We lost, but it was a good game.
cards.phrase: Perdimos, pero fue un buen partido.

cards.grammarNote:
**hacer** Literally 'to do/make'; many activities in Spanish use *hacer + noun*.
**el senderismo** The noun for hiking/trekking; comes from *senda* (path).
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey loves to hike in the mountains.
cards.phrase: A Jeffrey le encanta hacer senderismo en las montañas.

cards.grammarNote:
**el sendero** The specific word for a hiking trail or footpath.
**seguir** Use *seguir el sendero* (to follow the trail) — *seguir* is an *e→i* stem-changer.
cards.englishPhrase: The trail was steep but beautiful.
cards.phrase: El sendero era empinado pero hermoso.

cards.grammarNote:
**la montaña** Feminine noun; *las montañas* in the plural.
**subir** To go up a mountain use *subir la montaña*; *bajar* means to go down.
cards.englishPhrase: We reached the top of the mountain.
cards.phrase: Llegamos a la cima de la montaña.

cards.grammarNote:
**la mochila** Feminine noun; used for any backpack, not just hiking packs.
**llevar** *Llevar* means 'to carry' or 'to wear'; *llevo mi mochila* means 'I carry my backpack'.
cards.englishPhrase: My backpack has water and snacks.
cards.phrase: Mi mochila tiene agua y bocadillos.

cards.grammarNote:
**la bicicleta** The full word; *la bici* is the informal short form used in conversation.
**montar en bici** The standard phrase for 'to ride a bike'.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey rides his bike to the park.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey monta en bici hasta el parque.

cards.grammarNote:
**montar en** The verb *montar* means 'to mount/ride'; always paired with *en* for vehicles.
**andar en bici** An alternative in Latin America; both are understood everywhere.
cards.englishPhrase: I like to ride my bike on Sundays.
cards.phrase: Me gusta montar en bici los domingos.

cards.grammarNote:
**el casco** Used for bike helmets, motorcycle helmets, and hard hats.
**ponerse** Reflexive *ponerse el casco* means 'to put on the helmet'.
cards.englishPhrase: Always wear your helmet when you ride.
cards.phrase: Siempre ponte el casco cuando montes.

cards.grammarNote:
**la carrera** Means both 'race' (competition) and 'career/degree program' — context clarifies.
**correr una carrera** Literally 'to run a race'; used for cycling races too.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey finished the race in first place.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey terminó la carrera en primer lugar.

cards.grammarNote:
**hacer ejercicio** No article before *ejercicio* in this fixed phrase.
**el ejercicio** With an article it refers to a specific exercise or drill.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey exercises every morning before work.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey hace ejercicio todas las mañanas antes del trabajo.

cards.grammarNote:
**el entrenamiento** Derived from *entrenar* (to train/coach); the noun form.
**sesión de entrenamiento** A longer phrase meaning 'training session', very common in gyms.
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday's workout was really tough.
cards.phrase: El entrenamiento de ayer fue muy duro.

cards.grammarNote:
**estirar** Transitive: *estirar las piernas* (to stretch your legs).
**estirarse** Reflexive form meaning 'to stretch oneself'; used when no object is named.
cards.englishPhrase: I always stretch before a bike ride.
cards.phrase: Siempre me estiro antes de montar en bici.

cards.grammarNote:
**sudar** Regular -ar verb meaning 'to sweat'.
**sudar la camiseta** An idiomatic phrase meaning 'to work very hard' (lit. 'to sweat the shirt').
cards.englishPhrase: I sweat a lot during the tournament.
cards.phrase: Sudé mucho durante el torneo.

cards.grammarNote:
**el árbitro** Masculine form; *la árbitra* is the feminine form.
**pitar** The verb 'to referee/whistle a call' — *el árbitro pitó una falta* (the ref called a foul).
cards.englishPhrase: The referee made a bad call.
cards.phrase: El árbitro tomó una mala decisión.

cards.grammarNote:
**el estadio** A direct cognate with English 'stadium'; masculine noun.
**en el estadio** Use *en* for location inside or at the stadium.
cards.englishPhrase: There were thousands of people at the stadium.
cards.phrase: Había miles de personas en el estadio.

cards.grammarNote:
**el entrenador** From *entrenar* (to train); add *-a* ending for feminine.
**el/la coach** The English word *coach* is also widely used in Latin American sports contexts.
cards.englishPhrase: My coach says I need to practice my serve.
cards.phrase: Mi entrenador dice que necesito practicar mi saque.

cards.grammarNote:
**practicar** Used with sports names: *practicar el tenis* (to play tennis regularly).
**el entrenamiento** The session itself; *tenemos entrenamiento* means 'we have practice'.
cards.englishPhrase: We have practice on Tuesday and Thursday.
cards.phrase: Tenemos entrenamiento el martes y el jueves.

cards.grammarNote:
**el campeón** Masculine; *la campeona* is the feminine form; both are common.
**el campeonato** The related noun for 'championship' or 'championship tournament'.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey wants to be the pickleball champion.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey quiere ser el campeón de píckleball.

cards.grammarNote:
**el equipo** Also means 'equipment/gear'; context clarifies the meaning.
**jugar en equipo** 'To play as a team'; *trabajar en equipo* means 'to work as a team'.
cards.englishPhrase: My team played really well today.
cards.phrase: Mi equipo jugó muy bien hoy.

cards.grammarNote:
**el jugador** From *jugar* (to play); *-dor/-dora* is a common agent suffix.
**buen jugador** Adjectives agree with the noun: *una buena jugadora* for a female player.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey is the best player on the court.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey es el mejor jugador en la cancha.

cards.grammarNote:
**el empate** The noun for a tie result; *empatar* is the verb form.
**terminar en empate** To 'end in a tie'; *empatamos* means 'we tied'.
cards.englishPhrase: The game ended in a tie.
cards.phrase: El partido terminó en empate.

cards.grammarNote:
**la pelota** General word for a small ball; *el balón* is used for larger inflated balls.
**golpear la pelota** 'To hit the ball'; *golpear* is the verb for striking.
cards.englishPhrase: The ball went out of bounds.
cards.phrase: La pelota salió fuera de la línea.

cards.grammarNote:
**la red** Also means 'the internet' or 'the network' — context clarifies.
**pasar la red** 'To pass over the net'; *la pelota pasó la red* (the ball crossed the net).
cards.englishPhrase: My shot hit the net.
cards.phrase: Mi golpe golpeó la red.

cards.grammarNote:
**el/la atleta** One of the few Spanish nouns with the same form for both genders.
**deportista** Another word for an athlete or sportsperson, very common in everyday speech.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey is a dedicated athlete.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey es un atleta muy dedicado.

cards.grammarNote:
**el deporte** Masculine noun; *los deportes* in the plural.
**hacer deporte** The common phrase meaning 'to do sports / to be active'.
cards.englishPhrase: What is your favorite sport?
cards.phrase: ¿Cuál es tu deporte favorito?

cards.grammarNote:
**la competencia** Used in Latin America; Spain often says *la competición*.
**competir** The verb 'to compete'; it is an *e→i* stem-changing verb.
cards.englishPhrase: The competition starts at nine in the morning.
cards.phrase: La competencia empieza a las nueve de la mañana.

cards.grammarNote:
**entrenar** Regular -ar verb meaning 'to train' or 'to coach'.
**entrenarse** The reflexive form *entrenarse* means 'to train oneself / to work out'.
cards.englishPhrase: I trained hard all week for the tournament.
cards.phrase: Me entrené mucho toda la semana para el torneo.

cards.grammarNote:
**la velocidad** The noun for speed; *a gran velocidad* means 'at high speed'.
**rápido** An adjective (fast) that can also be used as an adverb meaning 'quickly'.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey bikes at high speed downhill.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey pedalea a gran velocidad cuesta abajo.

cards.grammarNote:
**cansado** An adjective; agrees with gender: *cansada* for feminine.
**cansarse** The reflexive verb 'to get/become tired'; *me canso* means 'I get tired'.
cards.englishPhrase: Bean got tired after five minutes on the trail.
cards.phrase: Bean se cansó después de cinco minutos en el sendero.

cards.grammarNote:
**la lesión** Feminine noun for an injury or strain.
**lesionarse** Reflexive verb meaning 'to injure oneself'; *me lesioné la rodilla* (I injured my knee).
cards.englishPhrase: I hope I don't get injured during the race.
cards.phrase: Espero no lesionarme durante la carrera.

cards.grammarNote:
**el agua** Feminine noun that takes *el* in the singular to avoid the double-vowel sound.
**hidratarse** Reflexive verb meaning 'to hydrate oneself'; important in sports context.
cards.englishPhrase: Remember to drink water during the hike.
cards.phrase: Recuerda beber agua durante la caminata.

cards.grammarNote:
**calentar** An *e→ie* stem-changer: *caliento*, *calientas*…; used for warming up.
**el calentamiento** The warm-up session itself; *hacer el calentamiento* (to do the warm-up).
cards.englishPhrase: We always warm up before playing.
cards.phrase: Siempre calentamos antes de jugar.

cards.grammarNote:
**anotar** Common in Latin America for scoring a point or goal.
**marcar** Also widely used; *marcar un gol* (to score a goal), *marcar un punto* (to score a point).
cards.englishPhrase: My brother scored three points in a row.
cards.phrase: Mi hermano anotó tres puntos seguidos.

cards.grammarNote:
**al aire libre** A fixed phrase meaning 'outdoors' or 'in the open air'.
**deportes al aire libre** 'Outdoor sports'; no article change needed inside the phrase.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey prefers outdoor sports.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey prefiere los deportes al aire libre.

cards.grammarNote:
**la meta** Means both 'the finish line' and 'the goal/aim'; context clarifies.
**cruzar la meta** 'To cross the finish line'; *cruzar* is a regular -ar verb.
cards.englishPhrase: I crossed the finish line!
cards.phrase: ¡Crucé la meta!

cards.grammarNote:
**el código** Masculine noun; used broadly for source code or any written program.
**artículo definido** Spanish requires the definite article *el/la* even when speaking generally: *el código está bien* = 'the code is fine / code is fine.'
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey is reading the code carefully.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey está leyendo el código con cuidado.

cards.grammarNote:
**programar** Regular -ar infinitive; conjugates like *hablar*.
**Jeffrey programa** Third-person present: drop -ar, add -a — *él programa* = 'he codes.'
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey likes to program at night.
cards.phrase: A Jeffrey le gusta programar de noche.

cards.grammarNote:
**el software** Spanish borrowed this word directly from English; it is masculine.
**loanwords** Many tech terms are English loanwords in Spanish and are used as-is, pronounced with a Spanish accent.
cards.englishPhrase: The new software is ready to deploy.
cards.phrase: El nuevo software está listo para desplegar.

cards.grammarNote:
**el ingeniero** Masculine form; feminine is *la ingeniera*.
**profesiones** In Spanish, job titles agree in gender with the person: Jeffrey is *el ingeniero*, a female colleague would be *la ingeniera*.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey is a software engineer.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey es ingeniero de software.

cards.grammarNote:
**el desarrollador** From *desarrollar* (to develop); feminine is *la desarrolladora*.
**-dor suffix** This suffix marks the agent who performs an action, like English '-er': *desarrollador* = developer, *programador* = programmer.
cards.englishPhrase: He is a senior developer on the team.
cards.phrase: Él es un desarrollador senior en el equipo.

cards.grammarNote:
**la computadora** Used in Latin America; Spain uses *el ordenador* (masculine).
**regional variation** Both terms are correct; context tells you which dialect you're hearing.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey's computer has three monitors.
cards.phrase: La computadora de Jeffrey tiene tres monitores.

cards.grammarNote:
**la laptop** Common in Latin America; borrowed from English.
**el portátil** Preferred in Spain; from *portátil* (portable). Both are widely understood.
cards.englishPhrase: Bean sits next to the laptop while Jeffrey works.
cards.phrase: Bean se sienta junto a la laptop mientras Jeffrey trabaja.

cards.grammarNote:
**el teclado** From *tecla* (key); masculine noun.
**compound meaning** *Tecla* = key, *-ado* = collective suffix — literally 'the keyed thing / key board.'
cards.englishPhrase: Bean stepped on the keyboard and deleted the code.
cards.phrase: Bean pisó el teclado y borró el código.

cards.grammarNote:
**la pantalla** Covers screen, monitor, and display; feminine noun.
**context clues** *la pantalla del teléfono* = phone screen, *la pantalla del servidor* = server display — same word, context clarifies.
cards.englishPhrase: The error appeared on the screen.
cards.phrase: El error apareció en la pantalla.

cards.grammarNote:
**el bug** Direct English borrowing; used widely in tech Spanish.
**el error** The more formal/native Spanish term; both refer to a software defect and are interchangeable in tech contexts.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey found a bug in production.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey encontró un bug en producción.

cards.grammarNote:
**depurar** Literally 'to purify'; the standard Spanish verb for debugging.
**present tense** *Yo depuro, tú depuras, él/ella depura* — regular -ar conjugation.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey is debugging the code right now.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey está depurando el código ahora mismo.

cards.grammarNote:
**arreglar** 'To fix / repair'; regular -ar verb.
**un error** Indefinite article *un* is used when introducing the bug for the first time; once established, use *el error*.
cards.englishPhrase: He needs to fix the bug before the deadline.
cards.phrase: Tiene que arreglar el error antes de la fecha límite.

cards.grammarNote:
**desplegar** Formal verb meaning 'to deploy/unfold'; used in technical documentation.
**hacer un deploy** Informal but very common in spoken tech Spanish — mixing English 'deploy' with *hacer* (to do/make).
cards.englishPhrase: We are going to deploy the app tomorrow.
cards.phrase: Vamos a desplegar la aplicación mañana.

cards.grammarNote:
**el servidor** From *servir* (to serve); masculine noun ending in -or.
**plural** *los servidores* — add -es to nouns ending in a consonant.
cards.englishPhrase: The server went down during the deploy.
cards.phrase: El servidor se cayó durante el deploy.

cards.grammarNote:
**la base de datos** Literally 'the base of data'; feminine noun phrase.
**de** The preposition *de* links nouns to show composition or purpose: *base de datos*, *ingeniero de software*, *reunión de equipo*.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey is setting up the database for the new project.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey está configurando la base de datos para el nuevo proyecto.

cards.grammarNote:
**la aplicación** Feminine noun; plural *las aplicaciones*.
**written accent** The accent on *ó* marks stress and distinguishes *aplicación* (noun) from the verb form *aplique* (apply).
cards.englishPhrase: The application crashed after the update.
cards.phrase: La aplicación se cayó después de la actualización.

cards.grammarNote:
**el sitio web** *Sitio* (site) is masculine; *web* is used as an adjective here.
**la página web** Also common for 'website' or 'web page'; either works.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey updated the company website.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey actualizó el sitio web de la empresa.

cards.grammarNote:
**la función** Means both 'function' (programming) and 'feature / role'.
**context** In code: *una función que devuelve un número* = 'a function that returns a number.' As feature: *una función nueva* = 'a new feature.'
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey wrote a function to process the data.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey escribió una función para procesar los datos.

cards.grammarNote:
**la característica** More precisely 'feature/characteristic'; common in product discussions.
**distinction** *La función* = function in code; *la característica* = product feature on a roadmap.
cards.englishPhrase: The team approved the new feature.
cards.phrase: El equipo aprobó la nueva característica.

cards.grammarNote:
**el pull request** English term used as-is in Spanish tech; masculine because *el request* is masculine by convention.
**la PR** Informally shortened to *la PR* (feminine, matching *la solicitud* = the request).
cards.englishPhrase: Can you review my pull request?
cards.phrase: ¿Puedes revisar mi pull request?

cards.grammarNote:
**la reunión** From *reunirse* (to meet/gather); feminine noun.
**accent** The accent on *ó* keeps stress on the last syllable — important for pronunciation.
cards.englishPhrase: The meeting starts in five minutes.
cards.phrase: La reunión empieza en cinco minutos.

cards.grammarNote:
**el standup** Direct English borrowing; used as-is in many tech companies in Spain and Latin America.
**la reunión diaria** Literal translation; used in more formal or fully Spanish-speaking workplaces.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey has standup at nine every morning.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey tiene el standup a las nueve cada mañana.

cards.grammarNote:
**la fecha límite** Literally 'the limit date'; *fecha* (date) is feminine.
**el plazo** Shorter synonym for deadline or time limit; common in formal writing.
cards.englishPhrase: The deadline is Friday at midnight.
cards.phrase: La fecha límite es el viernes a medianoche.

cards.grammarNote:
**el cliente** Can mean client (business), customer, or client-side (tech context).
**el lado del cliente** 'Client-side' in web development; *el lado del servidor* = 'server-side.'
cards.englishPhrase: The client wants the feature done by Friday.
cards.phrase: El cliente quiere la característica lista para el viernes.

cards.grammarNote:
**trabajar desde casa** Literally 'to work from home'; no article before *casa* in this fixed phrase.
**el trabajo remoto** The noun form: 'remote work.' *Trabajo* (work) is masculine.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey works from home every day.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey trabaja desde casa todos los días.

cards.grammarNote:
**el trabajo remoto** *Trabajo* = work/job; *remoto* = remote. Adjective follows noun.
**adjective agreement** *Remoto* is masculine to match *trabajo*; a feminine noun would require *remota*.
cards.englishPhrase: He loves remote work.
cards.phrase: Le encanta el trabajo remoto.

cards.grammarNote:
**la terminal** Feminine noun in computing contexts (also 'airport terminal').
**el terminal** Some speakers use the masculine; feminine is more standard for the command-line terminal.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey opened the terminal to run the tests.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey abrió la terminal para ejecutar las pruebas.

cards.grammarNote:
**la variable** Feminine noun; used identically to English.
**declaration** *Declarar una variable* = 'to declare a variable' — *declarar* is a regular -ar verb.
cards.englishPhrase: He forgot to declare the variable.
cards.phrase: Olvidó declarar la variable.

cards.grammarNote:
**el repositorio** From Latin *repositorium*; masculine noun.
**el repo** Informal shortening used in conversation, just as in English.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey pushed the code to the repository.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey subió el código al repositorio.

cards.grammarNote:
**la rama** Literally 'branch' (as in a tree); used directly for git branches.
**crear una rama** 'To create a branch' — *crear* is a regular -ar verb.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey created a new branch for the feature.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey creó una nueva rama para la característica.

cards.grammarNote:
**revisar** Regular -ar verb; means to review, check, or inspect.
**code review** *La revisión de código* is the noun phrase; *revisar el código* is the verb phrase.
cards.englishPhrase: Can you review the code before the meeting?
cards.phrase: ¿Puedes revisar el código antes de la reunión?

cards.grammarNote:
**las pruebas** Plural of *la prueba* (test/proof); feminine.
**pasar las pruebas** 'To pass the tests' — *pasar* can mean to pass, to go through, or to happen.
cards.englishPhrase: All tests are passing.
cards.phrase: Todas las pruebas están pasando.

cards.grammarNote:
**la actualización** From *actualizar* (to update); feminine noun with accent on final syllable.
**actualizar** Regular -ar verb: *actualizo, actualizas, actualiza, actualizamos...*
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey pushed an update to the codebase.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey subió una actualización al código base.

cards.grammarNote:
**el error crítico** *Crítico* is an adjective that follows the noun and agrees in gender.
**accented i** The accent on *í* in *crítico* marks stress on that syllable.
cards.englishPhrase: There is a critical error in production.
cards.phrase: Hay un error crítico en producción.

cards.grammarNote:
**la producción** Direct translation; feminine noun.
**en producción** 'In production' — no article after *en* in this fixed tech phrase.
cards.englishPhrase: Never push broken code to production.
cards.phrase: Nunca subas código roto a producción.

cards.grammarNote:
**el equipo** Masculine noun; also means 'equipment' — context distinguishes.
**mi equipo** 'My team'; possessive adjectives agree with the noun, not the owner.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey's team has a standup every morning.
cards.phrase: El equipo de Jeffrey tiene un standup cada mañana.

cards.grammarNote:
**el proyecto** Masculine noun; from Latin *projectus*.
**lanzar un proyecto** 'To launch a project' — *lanzar* (to launch/throw) is a regular -ar verb.
cards.englishPhrase: The new project starts next week.
cards.phrase: El nuevo proyecto empieza la próxima semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**lanzar** Regular -ar verb meaning to launch, release, or throw.
**lanzamos** First-person plural: 'we launch/release' — used often in standup: *lanzamos la versión hoy*.
cards.englishPhrase: We are going to launch the new version today.
cards.phrase: Vamos a lanzar la nueva versión hoy.

cards.grammarNote:
**la versión** Feminine noun; plural *las versiones*.
**versión dos punto cero** '2.0' is read as *dos punto cero* in Spanish.
cards.englishPhrase: Version two is ready for testing.
cards.phrase: La versión dos está lista para las pruebas.

cards.grammarNote:
**configurar** Regular -ar verb; used for setting up environments, tools, and systems.
**la configuración** Noun form: 'the configuration/setup'; feminine.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey configured the server this morning.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey configuró el servidor esta mañana.

cards.grammarNote:
**el entorno** Masculine noun meaning 'environment' or 'surroundings.'
**el entorno de desarrollo** 'The development environment'; *de desarrollo* (of development) modifies *entorno*.
cards.englishPhrase: The bug only appears in the production environment.
cards.phrase: El bug solo aparece en el entorno de producción.

cards.grammarNote:
**ejecutar** Regular -ar verb; 'to execute' a program or command.
**corre / correr** Informal alternative: *correr el código* = 'to run the code' — very common in spoken Spanish.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey ran the script from the terminal.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey ejecutó el script desde la terminal.

cards.grammarNote:
**el log** Direct English borrowing; masculine.
**los logs** Plural form; *revisar los logs* = 'to check the logs' is a common phrase.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey checked the logs to find the error.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey revisó los logs para encontrar el error.

cards.grammarNote:
**subir** Literally 'to go up / upload'; used for pushing code to a repo.
**hacer push** English loanword alternative: *hacer un push* = 'to do a push' — equally common in tech teams.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey pushed the code to the main branch.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey subió el código a la rama principal.

cards.grammarNote:
**la integración** Feminine noun; common in CI/CD discussions.
**la integración continua** 'Continuous integration' — *continua* agrees in gender with *integración*.
cards.englishPhrase: The continuous integration pipeline failed.
cards.phrase: El pipeline de integración continua falló.

cards.grammarNote:
**el comentario** Masculine noun; used for both code comments and conversational remarks.
**comentar el código** 'To comment the code' — *comentar* is a regular -ar verb.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey left a comment on the pull request.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey dejó un comentario en el pull request.

cards.grammarNote:
**necesitar** Regular -ar verb: *necesito, necesitas, necesita...*
**necesito más tiempo** 'I need more time' — *tiempo* is masculine.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey needs more time to fix the bug.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey necesita más tiempo para arreglar el bug.

cards.grammarNote:
**terminar** Regular -ar verb meaning 'to finish.'
**he terminado** Present perfect: 'I have finished' — formed with *haber* + past participle.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey finished the feature before the deadline.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey terminó la característica antes de la fecha límite.

cards.grammarNote:
**mazmorra** is feminine: **la mazmorra**, plural **las mazmorras** · From Arabic **al-mazmūra** (underground pit) — a classic Arabic borrowing in Spanish.
**oscura** (dark) is a feminine adjective agreeing with **mazmorra**: oscuro → oscura.
cards.englishPhrase: The dungeon is dark and dangerous.
cards.phrase: La mazmorra es oscura y peligrosa.

cards.grammarNote:
**dragón** is masculine: **el dragón**, plural **los dragones** · Accent on the final syllable; the plural drops the accent: **dragones** (stress shifts naturally).
**poderoso** (powerful) is a masculine adjective agreeing with **dragón**: poderosa would be feminine.
cards.englishPhrase: The dragon is very powerful.
cards.phrase: El dragón es muy poderoso.

cards.grammarNote:
**misión** is feminine: **la misión**, plural **las misiones** · Accent on the final syllable drops in the plural: **misión → misiones**.
**aceptar** (to accept) is a regular -ar verb; **aceptamos** = we accept (nosotros present tense).
cards.englishPhrase: We accept the quest.
cards.phrase: Aceptamos la misión.

cards.grammarNote:
**aventura** is feminine: **la aventura** · From Latin **adventura** (things about to happen) — same root as English 'adventure'.
**comenzar** (to begin) is an e→ie stem-changing verb: **comienza** = it begins (third-person singular).
cards.englishPhrase: The adventure begins at the tavern.
cards.phrase: La aventura comienza en la taberna.

cards.grammarNote:
**campaña** is feminine: **la campaña** · Used for a full D&D campaign (multi-session arc) as well as military campaigns.
**dirigir** (to run/direct) is an irregular yo form: **dirijo** (I direct) — g→j before o/a to preserve the soft /x/ sound.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey runs the campaign every weekend.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey dirige la campaña cada fin de semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**personaje** is masculine: **el personaje**, plural **los personajes** · From **persona** (person) + augmentative suffix **-aje** (borrowed from French -age).
**crear** (to create) is a regular -ar verb; **crear un personaje** = to create a character.
cards.englishPhrase: What character do you want to create?
cards.phrase: ¿Qué personaje quieres crear?

cards.grammarNote:
**mago** is masculine: **el mago**, feminine **la maga** · From Latin **magus** (wise man, magician) — same root as English 'mage' and 'magic'.
**lanza** (casts/throws) is the él/ella present of **lanzar** (to cast/throw) — a regular -ar verb.
cards.englishPhrase: The wizard casts a spell.
cards.phrase: El mago lanza un hechizo.

cards.grammarNote:
**guerrero** is masculine: **el guerrero**, feminine **la guerrera** · From **guerra** (war) — a Germanic borrowing in Spanish.
**proteger** (to protect) is a regular -er verb with a spelling change in the yo form: **protejo** (g→j before o to keep the soft /x/ sound).
cards.englishPhrase: The warrior protects the party.
cards.phrase: El guerrero protege al grupo.

cards.grammarNote:
**pícaro** is masculine: **el pícaro**, feminine **la pícara** · A classic Spanish literary archetype — the rogue/rascal hero of picaresque novels (genre named after **pícaro**).
**robar** (to steal) is a regular -ar verb; **robó** is the él/ella preterite: he/she stole.
cards.englishPhrase: The rogue stole the key from the guard.
cards.phrase: El pícaro le robó la llave al guardia.

cards.grammarNote:
**paladín** is masculine: **el paladín**, plural **los paladines** · From Latin **palatinus** (of the palace) — paladin knights were champions of Charlemagne.
**jurar** (to swear/vow) is a regular -ar verb; **jura** = he/she swears.
cards.englishPhrase: The paladin swears an oath of protection.
cards.phrase: El paladín jura un voto de protección.

cards.grammarNote:
**explorador** is masculine: **el explorador**, feminine **la exploradora** · Also called **el guardabosques** (forest warden) in D&D contexts — **bosque** = forest, **guardar** = to guard.
**preferir** (to prefer) is e→ie stem-changing: **prefiere** = he/she prefers.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey prefers to play a ranger.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey prefiere jugar de explorador.

cards.grammarNote:
**director del juego** is the official Spanish translation (game director/master) · **del** = contraction of **de + el** — mandatory in Spanish.
**Dungeon Master** is also widely used in Spanish D&D communities, often abbreviated **DM**.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey is the dungeon master tonight.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey es el director del juego esta noche.

cards.grammarNote:
**hechizo** is masculine: **el hechizo**, plural **los hechizos** · From **hechizar** (to bewitch/enchant) — related to **hecho** (done/made), suggesting spells as 'crafted things'.
**lanzar un hechizo** = to cast a spell — literally 'to throw a spell' (same as in English 'casting').
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey cast a fire spell on the goblin.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey lanzó un hechizo de fuego sobre el duende.

cards.grammarNote:
**conjuro** is masculine: **el conjuro** · A **conjuro** is an incantation or binding spell — slightly stronger/darker connotation than **hechizo** (a general spell).
**pronunciar** (to pronounce/utter) is a regular -ar verb; **pronunció** = he/she uttered (preterite).
cards.englishPhrase: The wizard uttered a powerful incantation.
cards.phrase: El mago pronunció un poderoso conjuro.

cards.grammarNote:
**magia** is feminine: **la magia** · From Greek **mageia** via Latin — the same Indo-European root as English 'magic'.
**encantado** (enchanted) is a past participle used as an adjective — agrees masculine with **bosque**: encantado/encantada/encantados/encantadas.
cards.englishPhrase: The forest is enchanted with ancient magic.
cards.phrase: El bosque está encantado con magia antigua.

cards.grammarNote:
**poción** is feminine: **la poción**, plural **las pociones** · From Latin **potio** (drink) — same root as English 'potion' and 'poison'.
**beber** (to drink) is a regular -er verb; **bebe** = he/she drinks. **la poción de vida** = health potion (literally 'potion of life').
cards.englishPhrase: Drink the health potion!
cards.phrase: ¡Bebe la poción de vida!

cards.grammarNote:
**espada** is feminine: **la espada**, plural **las espadas** · From Latin **spatha** (flat blade) — also gives us 'spade' in English card suits.
**desenvainó** = he/she drew (from the sheath) — preterite of **desenvainar** (to unsheathe), a regular -ar verb.
cards.englishPhrase: The warrior drew his sword.
cards.phrase: El guerrero desenvainó su espada.

cards.grammarNote:
**escudo** is masculine: **el escudo**, plural **los escudos** · Also the name of several Latin American currencies (historical) and national coats of arms — **el escudo nacional**.
**levantar** (to raise) is a regular -ar verb; **levantó** = he/she raised (preterite).
cards.englishPhrase: The paladin raised his shield.
cards.phrase: El paladín levantó su escudo.

cards.grammarNote:
**armadura** is feminine: **la armadura** · From **armar** (to arm) — related to **arma** (weapon) and Latin **armare**.
**pesada** (heavy) is a feminine adjective agreeing with **armadura**: pesado/pesada.
cards.englishPhrase: The warrior's armor is very heavy.
cards.phrase: La armadura del guerrero es muy pesada.

cards.grammarNote:
**dado** is masculine: **el dado** (one die), **los dados** (dice) · From **dar** (to give) — dice were originally 'given' by fate.
**tirar los dados** = to roll the dice — **tirar** literally means 'to throw', used in many games.
cards.englishPhrase: Roll the dice!
cards.phrase: ¡Tira los dados!

cards.grammarNote:
**tirar** (to roll/throw) is a regular -ar verb: **tiro, tiras, tira, tiramos, tiráis, tiran**.
**necesito que tires** uses the subjunctive (**tires**) because it expresses a wish/need directed at another person: **necesitar que + subjunctive** = to need someone to do something.
cards.englishPhrase: I need you to roll the dice now.
cards.phrase: Necesito que tires los dados ahora.

cards.grammarNote:
**golpe** is masculine: **el golpe** (hit/blow) · **crítico** is an adjective agreeing masculine with **golpe** — feminine would be **crítica**.
**¡Hiciste un golpe crítico!** — **hiciste** is the tú preterite of **hacer** (to do/make): hice, hiciste, hizo, hicimos, hicisteis, hicieron.
cards.englishPhrase: You got a critical hit!
cards.phrase: ¡Hiciste un golpe crítico!

cards.grammarNote:
**subir de nivel** = to level up — literally 'to rise in level' · **subir** (to go up/rise) is a regular -ir verb.
**subiste de nivel** is the tú preterite: **subir** → **subiste** (regular -ir preterite).
cards.englishPhrase: You leveled up! You are now level five.
cards.phrase: ¡Subiste de nivel! Ahora eres nivel cinco.

cards.grammarNote:
**puntos** is masculine plural: **los puntos** · Often abbreviated **PX** (puntos de experiencia) or **XP** in Spanish D&D communities.
**ganar** (to earn/win) is a regular -ar verb; **ganamos** = we earned (nosotros preterite — same form as present for -ar verbs).
cards.englishPhrase: We earned three hundred experience points.
cards.phrase: Ganamos trescientos puntos de experiencia.

cards.grammarNote:
**monstruo** is masculine: **el monstruo**, plural **los monstruos** · From Latin **monstrum** (omen, monster) — same root as English 'monster' and 'demonstrate'.
**apareció** is the preterite of **aparecer** (to appear) — an -er verb with yo spelling change: **aparezco**.
cards.englishPhrase: A monster appeared in the shadows.
cards.phrase: Un monstruo apareció entre las sombras.

cards.grammarNote:
**duende** is masculine: **el duende**, plural **los duendes** · **Duende** also means 'elf', 'sprite', or 'a magical quality' in flamenco art (el duende flamenco).
**emboscar** (to ambush) is a regular -ar verb; **emboscó** = he/she/it ambushed (preterite).
cards.englishPhrase: The goblin ambushed the brothers.
cards.phrase: El duende emboscó a los hermanos.

cards.grammarNote:
**tesoro** is masculine: **el tesoro**, plural **los tesoros** · From Latin **thesaurus** (storehouse) — same root as English 'thesaurus'.
**encontramos** = we found — this is both the present and preterite nosotros form of **encontrar** (to find); context tells us it is past here.
cards.englishPhrase: We found the treasure in the dungeon.
cards.phrase: Encontramos el tesoro en la mazmorra.

cards.grammarNote:
**mapa** is masculine despite ending in -a: **el mapa** — one of the notable exceptions to the -a = feminine rule (also: **el día**, **el problema**).
**señala** = points to/shows (él/ella form of **señalar**, a regular -ar verb).
cards.englishPhrase: The map shows the entrance to the dungeon.
cards.phrase: El mapa señala la entrada a la mazmorra.

cards.grammarNote:
**taberna** is feminine: **la taberna** · From Latin **taberna** (shop, inn) — same root as English 'tavern' and 'taverna'.
**reunirse** (to meet up/gather) is a reflexive verb; **nos reunimos** = we gather/meet.
cards.englishPhrase: The group meets at the tavern every session.
cards.phrase: El grupo se reúne en la taberna cada sesión.

cards.grammarNote:
**grupo** is masculine: **el grupo** · **aventureros** (adventurers) is masculine plural — includes both men and mixed groups in Spanish.
**el partido de aventureros** is another option; **partido** can also mean 'political party' or a sports 'match' — context matters.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey and his brothers form an adventuring party.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey y sus hermanos forman un grupo de aventureros.

cards.grammarNote:
**encantado** is the past participle of **encantar** used as an adjective · It agrees in gender and number: **encantado/encantada/encantados/encantadas**.
**un arma encantada** — **arma** (weapon) is feminine but uses **el** in singular: **el arma** (like **el agua**). Here it is modified post-article so **encantada** agrees feminine.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey found an enchanted weapon.
cards.phrase: Jeffrey encontró un arma encantada.

cards.grammarNote:
**atacar** is a regular -ar verb with a spelling change in the preterite yo form: **ataqué** (c→qu before e to preserve the hard /k/ sound).
**¡Ataca!** is the tú affirmative imperative — for -ar verbs, drop the -s from the tú present: **atacas → ¡Ataca!**
cards.englishPhrase: Attack the dragon now!
cards.phrase: ¡Ataca al dragón ahora!

cards.grammarNote:
**huir** (to flee) is an irregular -ir verb — a spelling 'y' is inserted in most conjugated forms: **huyo, huyes, huye, huimos, huís, huyen**.
**¡Huye!** is the tú affirmative imperative: **huye**.
cards.englishPhrase: Run! There are too many goblins!
cards.phrase: ¡Huye! ¡Hay demasiados duendes!

cards.grammarNote:
**curar** is a regular -ar verb: **curo, curas, cura, curamos, curáis, curan**.
**quiero que el mago cure** uses the present subjunctive (**cure**) because **querer que** expresses a desire about another person's action — the key subjunctive trigger.
cards.englishPhrase: I want the wizard to heal the warrior.
cards.phrase: Quiero que el mago cure al guerrero.

cards.grammarNote:
**defender** is an e→ie stem-changing verb: **defiendo, defiendes, defiende, defendemos, defendéis, defienden**.
**defiende** (he/she/it defends) is the él/ella present — the stem vowel changes from e→ie in all persons except nosotros and vosotros.
cards.englishPhrase: The paladin defends the group.
cards.phrase: El paladín defiende al grupo.

cards.grammarNote:
**explorar** is a regular -ar verb · From Latin **explorare** (to investigate) — same root as English 'explore'.
**exploramos** = we explore — nosotros present tense of **explorar**.
cards.englishPhrase: We explore the dungeon carefully.
cards.phrase: Exploramos la mazmorra con cuidado.

cards.grammarNote:
**puntos de vida** = hit points (literally 'life points') · **vida** is feminine: **la vida**.
**tengo** is the irregular yo form of **tener** (to have): tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen.
cards.englishPhrase: I only have five hit points left.
cards.phrase: Solo tengo cinco puntos de vida.

cards.grammarNote:
**turno** is masculine: **el turno**, plural **los turnos** · Used in board games, card games, and D&D for whose turn it is.
**Es tu turno** = It's your turn — **ser** is used for stating whose turn it is (a factual identity/assignment).
cards.englishPhrase: It's your turn to attack.
cards.phrase: Es tu turno de atacar.

cards.grammarNote:
**victoria** is feminine: **la victoria** · From Latin **victoria** — same root as English 'victory'.
**logramos** = we achieved/managed — preterite of **lograr** (to achieve), a regular -ar verb.
cards.englishPhrase: We achieved a great victory.
cards.phrase: Logramos una gran victoria.

cards.grammarNote:
**enemigo** is masculine: **el enemigo**, feminine **la enemiga** · From Latin **inimicus** (unfriendly) — the prefix **in-** (not) + **amicus** (friend).
**cayó** is the preterite of **caer** (to fall) — irregular: caí, caíste, cayó, caímos, caísteis, cayeron.
cards.englishPhrase: The enemy fell after one hit.
cards.phrase: El enemigo cayó después de un golpe.

cards.grammarNote:
**trampa** is feminine: **la trampa**, plural **las trampas** · Also used figuratively: **¡Es una trampa!** (It's a trap!) — a classic phrase.
**caer en una trampa** = to fall into a trap — **caer** (to fall) is an irregular yo verb: **caigo**.
cards.englishPhrase: Careful, that's a trap!
cards.phrase: ¡Cuidado, es una trampa!

cards.grammarNote:
**botín** is masculine: **el botín** (loot/booty) · Also means 'ankle boot' in everyday Spanish — same word, very different contexts!
**repartir** (to distribute/divide) is a regular -ir verb; **repartimos** = we split (nosotros preterite).
cards.englishPhrase: We split the loot among the group.
cards.phrase: Repartimos el botín entre el grupo.

cards.grammarNote:
**posadero** is masculine: **el posadero**, feminine **la posadera** · From **posada** (inn/lodging) — **posar** means to rest/lodge.
**dar una misión** = to give a quest — **dio** is the él/ella preterite of **dar** (to give): di, diste, dio, dimos, disteis, dieron.
cards.englishPhrase: The innkeeper gave the adventurers a quest.
cards.phrase: El posadero le dio una misión a los aventureros.

cards.grammarNote:
**arco** is masculine: **el arco** · Also means 'arch' (architectural) and 'arc' — a versatile word.
**disparar** (to shoot) is a regular -ar verb; **disparó** = he/she shot (preterite). Jeffrey's ranger uses a bow as his signature weapon.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeffrey's ranger shot an arrow with his bow.
cards.phrase: El explorador de Jeffrey disparó una flecha con su arco.

cards.grammarNote:
**sesión** is feminine: **la sesión**, plural **las sesiones** · Accent on the final syllable drops in plural: **sesión → sesiones**.
**los sábados** = on Saturdays — plural definite article + day of week expresses a habitual action.
cards.englishPhrase: We play D&D on Saturdays.
cards.phrase: Jugamos a D&D los sábados.

cards.grammarNote:
**regla** is feminine: **la regla**, plural **las reglas** · Also means 'ruler' (measuring tool) — same word.
**discutir** (to discuss/argue) is a regular -ir verb; **discutimos** = we discuss/argue (nosotros present).
cards.englishPhrase: We always discuss the rules before the session.
cards.phrase: Siempre discutimos las reglas antes de la sesión.

cards.grammarNote:
**iniciativa** is feminine: **la iniciativa** · In D&D, **tirar iniciativa** = to roll for initiative — determines the order of combat turns.
**determina** = determines (él/ella present of **determinar**, a regular -ar verb).
cards.englishPhrase: Rolling initiative determines who goes first.
cards.phrase: Tirar iniciativa determina quién va primero.

cards.grammarNote:
**cara** is feminine: **la cara** (face/side of a die) · **dado de veinte caras** = twenty-faced die — Spanish describes dice by their face count.
Common in D&D communities: also simply called **el d20** (borrowed from English).
cards.englishPhrase: I rolled a twenty on the d20!
cards.phrase: ¡Saqué un veinte en el dado de veinte caras!

cards.englishPhrase: Yes, I would like a coffee, please.
